title: Sheetal Jaitly
tagline: A map of a sales-trained founder who built, nearly lost and rebuilt a software consultancy, and who now tells enterprises to redesign themselves around AI rather than bolt it on.
credit: An independent StoryTellr study by Nikhil Khedkar.
disclaimer: Built only from Sheetal Jaitly's publicly published professional record: his writing, interviews, press coverage and company pages. Personal and family details in those sources are deliberately left out. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Sheetal Jaitly or TribalScale.

nodes.title: Sheetal Jaitly
nodes.summary: Founder and CEO of TribalScale, a Toronto-based software and AI consultancy, and the author of a run of 2026 essays on becoming AI-native.
nodes.evidence: Founder and Chief Executive Officer @ TribalScale

nodes.title: Shipping desk at Keating
nodes.summary: His first tech job, per a magazine profile, was in shipping and receiving at Keating Technologies, where he watched a company scale fast.
nodes.details: The profile is undated, and the period is not given. Nothing earlier in his career could be confirmed from pages I read.
nodes.evidence: I saw what rapid growth from 30 to 300 people looked like.

nodes.title: Copiers, then analytics sales
nodes.summary: He learned to sell at Ricoh and was then recruited by a customer to sell predictive analytics, a product clients did not yet know they wanted.
nodes.details: The profile places this in the mid 2000s and says he was a director-level employee at 27 before joining Xtreme Labs. An Open Concept blurb separately mentions his time as a door-to-door photocopier salesman.
nodes.evidence: landed at Ricoh as a copy machine salesman

nodes.title: Xtreme Labs
nodes.summary: A Toronto mobile-app shop where he joined friends at its launch and, per the profile, helped grow revenue to $37.5m in five years.
nodes.details: The Globe and Mail describes Xtreme Labs as founded in 2007 by Amar Varma and Sundeep Madra with 350 staff in 2013; it does not mention Jaitly. His role and the $37.5m figure rest on the magazine profile alone. A 2025 podcast lists 'Xtreme Labs Experience and Mafia' among its topics.
nodes.evidence: helped grow the business to $37.5m in revenue in five years

nodes.title: Pivotal buys Xtreme Labs
nodes.summary: In October 2013 Pivotal bought Xtreme Labs; the profile says the company later passed to Dell, and that he struggled to find his place in the larger organisation.
nodes.details: The Globe reports the price was undisclosed and cites All Things Digital for $65 million (US). The Dell step is stated only in the profile.
nodes.evidence: Xtreme Labs was acquired by Pivotal, and then by Dell

nodes.title: TribalScale is founded
nodes.summary: He started the company in November 2015, saying he saw a gap in how organisations deliver digital products in an Agile way.
nodes.details: In the same profile he says that in a big organisation he felt like one person at a desk in a big machine, which he gives as a reason for leaving.
nodes.evidence: I first started TS because I saw there was a big gap in the market.

nodes.title: The $1.2m first client
nodes.summary: In his telling, a media-company buyer he had advised at Pivotal cut his pitch short and signed a $1.2m contract because he had once talked that buyer out of a bigger purchase.
nodes.details: The client is unnamed and the account is single-sourced to the magazine profile, so treat the figure as his account.
nodes.evidence: you rejected the opportunity for a huge commission just to do what was right by me.

nodes.title: 0 to 100 in two years
nodes.summary: By the second anniversary TribalScale reported 100+ employees and offices in Toronto, California and Dubai, the first stretch of fast growth.
nodes.details: TribalScale's own count at two years: over 125 members globally; a Dubai team of 14; new Toronto HQ at 200 Wellington St W. These are company statements.
nodes.evidence: In less than two years, we went from 0 to 100 employees.

nodes.title: TakeOver conference
nodes.summary: A conference he started because he wanted a less cookie-cutter tech event in Toronto; it grew from 800 attendees in 2017 to a sold-out 1,700 in 2018.
nodes.details: TribalScale says 83 speakers in 2017 (52% women) and that Prime Minister Justin Trudeau opened the 2018 event, which raised money for SickKids. BetaKit later reports a 2019 edition was cancelled, leaving a hotel claim in the insolvency filings.
nodes.evidence: We did our first TakeOver in 2017 with over 800 attendees.

nodes.title: Venture Studios
nodes.summary: A startup-creation arm announced in 2018 with a $100 million target, offering $500,000 in cash and support to accepted startups in blockchain, AI and voice.
nodes.details: Launched with chief innovation officer Roger Chabra; Kirstine Stewart joined as president and chief revenue officer around the announcement (BetaKit). TribalScale's site today still runs a Venture Studio and says 'Most venture studios advise. We build.'
nodes.evidence: create startups in the blockchain, AI, and voice space over the next five years

nodes.title: Voice and Alexa skills
nodes.summary: An early bet on voice interfaces: TribalScale said in 2017 that Amazon and Google recognised it as an expert builder for their voice platforms.
nodes.details: This is TribalScale's own claim; I found no Amazon or Google statement. The 2017 TakeOver programme also listed Voice among its topics.
nodes.evidence: Being recognized by Amazon and Google as expert Alexa skill and Action builders for their voice platforms

nodes.title: A large client leaves (2019)
nodes.summary: He dates the trouble to a large client restructuring and ending its engagement, leaving an oversized team; revenue concentrated in two clients.
nodes.details: BetaKit adds that, per Jaitly, a second client also hired away staff, and that debts began to build in early 2019. These are his explanations; the clients are not named.
nodes.evidence: We had a large client restructure their company and exit our engagement and we struggled to maintain our large staff capacity.

nodes.title: Insolvency filing, May 2020
nodes.summary: Independent trade press reported TribalScale filing a notice of intention under Canada's Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, a formal route to restructure rather than go bankrupt.
nodes.details: BetaKit, working from public filings, says the filing was May 19 and that the company's lawyer described a landlord's lease-default claim as the trigger. Jaitly told BetaKit the filing belonged to a restructuring plan begun over a year earlier. His own 2021 essay describes the landlord disagreement as what brought the company into CCAA protection.
nodes.evidence: TribalScale owes more than $5.8 million to 45 creditors

nodes.title: Pandemic shock, 2020
nodes.summary: The profile says the company lost most of its customers in early 2020 and he chose to keep serving clients at no charge; the Toronto office closed on March 16.
nodes.details: The 80% figure and the free reinvestment are the magazine's wording of what he said, not independently checked. BetaKit separately says the pandemic accelerated the filing timeline and ended a possible sale of the company (his claim).
nodes.evidence: The first months of 2020 saw TribalScale lose 80 percent of their customers.

nodes.title: Out of creditor protection
nodes.summary: The company says it exited its restructuring proceeding under Canada's CCAA on January 27, 2021 and describes itself as leaner and healthier.
nodes.details: The press release and his essay are the company's account; the terms of the restructuring were not read. The release also says the company 'closed over $81 million of funding in five years' (company claim, unclear what is counted).
nodes.evidence: TribalScale emerged from creditor protection on January 27, 2021.

nodes.title: The 'TribalScale 2.0' essay
nodes.summary: His own account of the reset: what went wrong, how the team shut the office, and why he calls the rebuilt company more sustainable.
nodes.details: Written by Jaitly as CEO and published on the company's Medium page; it frames the episode around resilience and ends with a pitch to clients.
nodes.evidence: Clawing our way out of creditor protection was the greatest and most difficult feat our company has ever faced.

nodes.title: Three sets of growth figures
nodes.summary: Sources give different numbers for the boom years, and none is independently verified, so this map does not pick one.
nodes.details: Profile: 'just over $50m in revenue', 250+ staff, seven offices in three years. BetaKit quoting Jaitly: $60 million over three years, $30 million in 2018. Company press release: 'over $81 million of funding in five years'. Headcount also appears as 125+ (Nov 2017) and about 60 (June 2020).
nodes.evidence: In three years, TribalScale earned just over $50m in revenue, grew the staff to 250+

nodes.title: Fail Fast
nodes.summary: A motto he hands out on stickers; he frames setbacks as something to learn from quickly, and used it again to describe the 2020 recovery.
nodes.evidence: Sheetal Jaitly gives his employees stickers that say “Fail Fast”.

nodes.title: Do right by the client
nodes.summary: A recurring claim in his own accounts: advising clients against a bigger sale, and later serving them free when revenue collapsed, pays back over time.
nodes.details: Both episodes are told by Jaitly via the magazine profile; neither was independently confirmed.
nodes.evidence: doing what’s right comes back to you exponentially when you develop the right bonds

nodes.title: Core values after the reset
nodes.summary: After exiting creditor protection he set out the company's values as Resilience, Empowerment, and Challenge & Collaborate.
nodes.evidence: Our next step was to define our Core Values.

nodes.title: 'Transparency' dropped
nodes.summary: In the profile he says he removed transparency from the core values because people used it as cover for attacks, replacing it with resiliency.
nodes.details: He adds the company is 'still transparent'; he objected to the word as a value, not to openness. The profile is undated.
nodes.evidence: The term was used to attack people.

nodes.title: Transparency on the site today
nodes.summary: The current Who We Are page lists Transparency again, beside Empowerment and Meritocracy; I found no source explaining the change.
nodes.details: The two sources are undated or differently dated, so this records a difference in wording, not a reversal or its cause. The page footer reads 2025.
nodes.evidence: Built on Empowerment, Meritocracy, Transparency

nodes.title: Friendly, not friends
nodes.summary: Citing a peer's 'rotten strawberry' idea, he says he now keeps a professional distance from staff and sees removing bad apples as important, having earlier tried to work through problems instead.
nodes.evidence: I have to be friendly – not friends – with my employees.

nodes.title: Redesign, don't add AI
nodes.summary: His headline argument: companies are buying copilots and running pilots but leaving workflows intact, and should instead redesign workflow, jobs, teams, product, stack, governance and measurement.
nodes.evidence: Most companies are adding 2026 AI to 2016 workflows.

nodes.title: The AI-native enterprise
nodes.summary: A twelve-point checklist that moves from copilots to agents, treats context as infrastructure and calls AI-native an operating-model change rather than a technology one.
nodes.evidence: Copilots help people perform tasks. Agents perform work.

nodes.title: Stop buying AI seats
nodes.summary: He argues per-employee AI licences rarely change how a business operates, and that AI should be built into the work so it becomes invisible.
nodes.evidence: Buying everyone an AI seat is not AI transformation.

nodes.title: Build vs buy, reopened
nodes.summary: Because AI lowers the cost of custom software, he says enterprises should weigh building the workflows that differentiate them instead of defaulting to SaaS.
nodes.details: He still says to buy standardised commodity capabilities; the essay includes a buy/build comparison table.
nodes.evidence: This is why I am increasingly bullish on building custom software again.

nodes.title: Governed autonomy
nodes.summary: Agents that act inside enterprise systems need identity, permissions, audit and approval designed in from the start, not added after a pilot works.
nodes.evidence: Governance therefore has to move into the architecture.

nodes.title: Measure leverage, not activity
nodes.summary: If agents do the repetitive work, he says the useful question about an employee changes from what they did to what they built that keeps producing results.
nodes.evidence: Companies should begin measuring leverage—not activity.

nodes.title: Be your own AI case study
nodes.summary: Point twelve of his list: a firm that sells AI advice should run its own operations on AI first. TribalScale's site lists an internal enterprise agentic platform among its cases.
nodes.details: The How We Work page lists a case titled 'Building an Enterprise Agentic Platform for Delivery, Operations, and Personal Productivity'; I read only the title, not the case.
nodes.evidence: Use AI internally. Aggressively.

nodes.title: FinScale Magazine
nodes.summary: A free digital magazine for financial-services and insurance leaders, launched in May 2025, where several of his later pieces first appeared.
nodes.evidence: AI, data, and digital transformation are no longer future-focused buzzwords

nodes.title: The deployment gap
nodes.summary: He argues the coming failures in financial-services AI will be agent projects that reach production and then fail silently, which old monitoring does not catch.
nodes.details: Only the introduction is public; the rest is gated behind a FinScale download. It cites a VentureBeat analysis from April 2026 that I did not read.
nodes.evidence: is the service behaving correctly?

nodes.title: The insurance AI gap
nodes.summary: An essay opening with an unnamed insurer executive's complaint that most of her firm's AI initiatives are not in production, then arguing insurance lags banking.
nodes.details: The statistics (McKinsey 2024, Deloitte, Accenture) are quoted by him from third parties and were not checked. Only the introduction is public.
nodes.evidence: fewer than 10 percent of P&C and life insurers have deployed AI at scale

nodes.title: Feed Ontario and SickKids
nodes.summary: His company profile lists a board seat at Feed Ontario and membership of the Tech4SickKids Council.
nodes.details: Self-described and undated; I found no independent listing of either role or their dates. Separately, TakeOver 2018 raised money for SickKids.
nodes.evidence: Sheetal is a board member of Feed Ontario, a member of Tech4SickKids Council

nodes.title: DMZ and Techstars
nodes.summary: The same profile lists him as a DMZ member and a Techstars mentor, tying him to Toronto's startup support ecosystem.
nodes.details: Self-described and undated; not independently confirmed.
nodes.evidence: DMZ, and a TechStars Mentor

nodes.title: Harvard OPM program
nodes.summary: A Harvard Business School programme for owner-presidents, which he discusses on the company podcast and which a magazine profile says he was enrolled in.
nodes.details: Enrolment dates and completion are not stated in the sources I read.
nodes.evidence: the Owner/President Management Program at Harvard Business School

nodes.title: First Name Basis podcast
nodes.summary: TribalScale's own interview podcast; in episode 64 a marketing coordinator interviews him about learning and working in teams.
nodes.evidence: Episode 64, 27 min

nodes.title: Outside interviews
nodes.summary: Third-party podcasts and shows from 2018 to 2025, on innovation, digital transformation and building a services business.
nodes.details: Read as show notes only: The Business Leadership Podcast (Jan 2018), Open Concept (undated), MarketScale on Industry 4.0 (Nov 2022), The Hard Part with Evan McCann (Apr 2025).
nodes.evidence: The things that we thought were impossible are now being shown to us that they can be possible.

nodes.title: 'Top 10 Leading Men' (MSN)
nodes.summary: TribalScale's press release says an MSN global profile named him one of ten leading men of 2025; I could not find the MSN piece itself.
nodes.details: Treat as a company claim; the feature may be sponsored or syndicated.
nodes.evidence: named one of the Top 10 Leading Men in 2025 in MSN

stories.title: From the sales floor to founder
stories.summary: A career that moved from shipping desks to copiers to analytics to a mobile studio, ending in his own company. The profile ties the start to one principle he repeats: advise the client even when it costs you a sale.

stories.title: Boom, filing, reset
stories.summary: Fast growth, a big-client loss, an insolvency filing made worse by the pandemic, and an exit in January 2021. Sources disagree on the boom-year numbers, so the sequence is firmer than the figures.

stories.title: How the values moved
stories.summary: A motto, a rebuild, a value dropped and a value that seems to have returned. Only the wording is documented; the reasons behind the later wording are not.

stories.title: From rebuilding a company to redesigning one
stories.summary: The editorial thread of this map: after rebuilding his own firm he argues others should redesign theirs. The middle links are dashed because no source connects them; it is a reading, not a finding.

stories.title: Agents in regulated industries
stories.summary: His 2026 financial-services pieces extend the redesign argument into governance: autonomy is useful only if actions stay visible and bounded, and failures may be silent.
